extracted.intended_audience: general readers of Montaigne; readers interested in moral/philosophical essays and practical maxims
extracted.subtask_short: personal essay on custom and health
extracted.subtask_description: A reflective personal essay (Montaigne-style) discussing self-knowledge, the effects of custom, conduct of life, speech, and approaches to health and physicians. The page is a literary-philosophical meditation rather than an instructional manual.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prudence as execution of 'know thyself'
rubrics_metrics.description: Prudence consists in carrying out the Delphic ordinance to know oneself; recognizing the extent of one's ignorance is a prerequisite to true inquiry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plato and Socrates are invoked: difficulties and obscurities are only discerned by those within a science; a degree of intelligence is required to know that one does not know. This yields modesty and moderation of opinion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid assertion before knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: Affirmation and obstinacy are express signs of want of wit; assertion and decision should not precede knowledge and perception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cicero quoted: 'Nothing is worse than that assertion and decision should precede knowledge and perception.' Examples: the incorrigible coxcomb who repeats his assertions despite contrary experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of long self-examination
rubrics_metrics.description: Sustained attention to one's own life enables more accurate judgment of others and cultivates modesty, obedience of belief, and measured opinions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author reports that contemplating his own life has let him notice qualities in friends, warn them, and learn; this habit gives a particular aptitude for judging others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Who may rightly examine another's soul
rubrics_metrics.description: One who would examine the soul of another must have three qualities: knowledge, benevolence, and boldness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plato's requirement: the examiner should be knowledgeable to judge, benevolent so as not to malign, and bold enough to speak honestly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Qualities required of a confidential adviser to a prince
rubrics_metrics.description: A person giving free and faithful advice to a sovereign should be content with his own fortune, of moderate station, limited to one such office, and above all keep fidelity of silence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reasons: contentment prevents fear of losing preferment; moderate station allows easier communication with many; limiting the office to one person avoids irreverence; silence preserves the master's privacy. Also requires courage because favourites tend to protect their own interests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Truth has circumspection and limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Truth is not to be spoken indiscriminately at all times; even virtuous remonstrance can be injuriously or unjustly applied.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Speaking truth requires judgment about timing, manner, and likely application; blunt truth can do harm if ill-applied.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain accustomed habits in sickness
rubrics_metrics.description: Keep the same form of life in sickness as in health: same bed, same hours, same food and drink, adjusting only moderation; radical change distempers and disturbs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author's practice: minimal change between health and sickness; custom shapes bodily tolerance so sudden contrary prescriptions can harm (examples: sleeping, meals, bed, napkin habits).

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect patient's customs and constitution in medical treatment
rubrics_metrics.description: Medical rules should be modified according to climates, constitutions, and established habits; physicians differ and one regimen does not fit all.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The art of physic is not fixed; references to differing authorities (Fernel, Scaliger) and anecdotes (Tiberius governing his health without physicians) illustrate that treatments must fit the patient's nature and customs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permit Nature to take its course; avoid over-treatment
rubrics_metrics.description: One should neither obstinately oppose evils nor yield without courage; often diseases resolve by their own course and excessive intervention or multiple physicians may lengthen or worsen illness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author's observation: some maladies went away without art; attempting to cut short course of disease can lengthen it; example of those who had three physicians and still died.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer remedies that are pleasant and not worse than the disease
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid remedies more troublesome than the disease itself; if a medicine is pleasant and agreeable, take it—pleasure is a chief kind of profit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author dislikes cures that add suffering; satisfying certain longings during sickness can be beneficial, and he often allows pleasure to guide medical choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Speak in tone and manner suited to the affair and auditor
rubrics_metrics.description: Adjust voice and tone according to the matter and the receiver: there are voices to instruct, to flatter, and to reprehend; speaking properly is partly the speaker's responsibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anecdote of Greek school and Quintilian quoted: 'Speak according to the affair you are speaking about to your auditor.' The tone can be made to strike or pierce; it is not merely enough that the listener hears.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultivate flexibility rather than rigid rule-following
rubrics_metrics.description: A life carried strictly by rule is weak; young men should sometimes cross their own rules to awaken vigor; over-fastidiousness and inflexibility are serious faults.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author endorses adaptability—custom should make us pliable; a soldier especially must be able to endure variety and inequality of life. Quoted Juvenal and examples of habits and customs illustrate this point.

rubrics_metrics.name: Friendship sometimes requires wounding honesty
rubrics_metrics.description: True friendship may demand the courage to wound and offend for the friend's own good; this frank criticism is an effect of sincere friendship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hearing frank criticism requires 'sound ears'; one who ventures to criticise does a singular service and demonstrates real affection by risking displeasure.
